---
title: "Reference selection"
subtitle: "Module 2 — 30 min"
---

## Why it matters

Reads are mapped to **one** reference, and the consensus is built from that mapping. A reference that is too
divergent causes reads to map badly (or not at all), hides real variants and biases the consensus towards the reference.

| Criterion | Question |
|---|---|
| Same species/genotype | is it the right virus, and the right segment/genotype? |
| Close to your samples | few differences = better mapping |
| Complete and good quality | no gaps or ambiguous bases |
| Well annotated, traceable | accession, source, date |
| Consistent across the study | use **the same** reference for all samples being compared |

## Exercise

Three candidate references are in `data/reference/candidates/`: `TOYV1_TV1` (root genotype), `TOYV1_TV2`
(a genotype that appeared later) and `TOYV2_divergent` (another, more distant virus).

1. Compare your S01 consensus with each candidate:
   ```bash
   python3 scripts/10_pick_reference.py results/consensus/S01.fa
   ```
   (plan B: `precomputed/consensus/S01.fa`)
2. Which reference is the closest? How many mismatches? Does it match what you expect from the lineage story?
3. Re-map S01 on a farther candidate and compare the % mapped and mean depth:
   ```bash
   REF=data/reference/candidates/TOYV2_divergent.fasta RESULTS=results_div bash scripts/run_all.sh S01
   ```

::: {.callout-note}
## In real life
The choice is made with databases (e.g. NCBI Virus, GISAID-type resources, Nextclade datasets) and a quick
identity search. Small differences between close references matter less than choosing the wrong genotype.
:::

**Question:** why should all samples of an outbreak be mapped to the same reference?
